findings.title: Hardcoded SQL Server 'sa' credential (sa/tss.123) committed across ~40 Python bootstrap scripts
findings.cvss: CVSS 5.5 (local/dev-only credential, but committed to VCS and grants full DB sysadmin if the same password is reused in any reachable environment) — risk hinges on credential reuse
findings.description: The SQL Server system administrator credential `sa` / `tss.123` is hard-coded as a literal in the pyodbc connection string of roughly 40 repository-root and `.tools/` Python scripts (setup_*.py, seed_*.py, fix_*.py). All of these files are tracked in git (`git ls-files` confirms they are committed, and none are matched by `.gitignore`). `sa` is the highest-privilege account on a SQL Server instance — full control of every database, ability to read/alter all tenant data, enable xp_cmdshell, etc. While CLAUDE.md documents `sa/tss.123` as the intentional local-dev account, the password is a real, weak, reused secret that now lives permanently in repository history. The concrete risk is credential reuse: if any developer, CI runner, or shared/staging SQL Server instance is provisioned with the same `sa` password (a very common shortcut), this commit hands an attacker sysadmin access to that instance.
findings.rootCause: Connection secrets were inlined as string literals in dev tooling instead of being read from environment variables (the backend already does this via `${DB_PASSWORD}`), so the password is duplicated into ~40 files and baked into git history.
findings.impact: Anyone with read access to the repository (or its history) obtains a working sysadmin SQL Server credential. If `tss.123` is reused on any networked/staging instance, this is full database compromise: cross-tenant data exfiltration, tampering, and potential OS command execution via xp_cmdshell. Even confined to localhost dev, it normalises committing real passwords and makes secret rotation impossible without history rewrite.
findings.reproduction: 1. `git log -p -- seed_real_data.py` (or any setup_*.py) shows `UID=sa;PWD=tss.123` in the connection string. 2. From any host that can reach a SQL Server provisioned with this password: `sqlcmd -S <host> -U sa -P tss.123 -Q "SELECT name FROM sys.databases"` succeeds with sysadmin rights.
findings.resolution: Read the connection string from environment variables in every script (e.g. a shared `db_conn()` helper that reads `DB_PASSWORD`, defaulting only for local dev). Rotate the dev `sa` password and never reuse it outside localhost. Add a pre-commit secret scanner (gitleaks/trufflehog). Treat history scrubbing as optional for a dev-only password but mandatory if `tss.123` is ever used beyond a throwaway local instance.
findings.patchBefore:
CONN_STR = (
    'DRIVER={ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server};SERVER=localhost;DATABASE=TSS_GRC;'
    'UID=sa;PWD=tss.123;Unicode_Results=Yes;'
)
conn = pyodbc.connect(CONN_STR)
findings.patchAfter:
import os
CONN_STR = (
    "DRIVER={ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server};"
    f"SERVER={os.environ.get('DB_HOST','localhost')};DATABASE={os.environ.get('DB_NAME','TSS_GRC')};"
    f"UID={os.environ.get('DB_USERNAME','sa')};PWD={os.environ['DB_PASSWORD']};Unicode_Results=Yes;"
)
conn = pyodbc.connect(CONN_STR)
# DB_PASSWORD must be exported; no default so an unconfigured run fails loudly.
references: OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures

findings.title: TLS certificate validation disabled in DB connections (TrustServerCertificate / Encrypt=No)
findings.cvss: CVSS 3.7 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — MITM exposure on the DB channel; localhost-only in practice for the dev scripts, but the prod JDBC default also trusts any cert
findings.description: The base/dev JDBC URL uses `encrypt=true;trustServerCertificate=true`, which encrypts the channel but disables certificate validation, defeating MITM protection. The ~14 Python scripts that connect via ODBC use `TrustServerCertificate=yes` or `Encrypt=No`, which similarly disable validation (or encryption entirely). For the localhost dev scripts the practical exposure is negligible, but the same `trustServerCertificate=true` pattern is carried in the base `application.yml` datasource URL that the prod profile's documented `DB_URL` comment also references — meaning an operator copying the example connects to the production database over a channel that trusts any presented certificate.
findings.rootCause: Certificate trust was disabled to avoid configuring a CA/trust store during local development, and the insecure setting was left in the base configuration and the prod URL example rather than scoped strictly to dev.
findings.impact: An attacker positioned between the application (or a script) and the SQL Server can present a forged certificate and transparently intercept/modify all database traffic, including the `sa` login and every tenant's data. Risk is high only on untrusted networks; on localhost it is informational.
findings.reproduction: 1. Inspect application.yml:15 and the prod DB_URL example comment (application-prod.yml:9). 2. Note `trustServerCertificate=true` (Java) and `TrustServerCertificate=yes`/`Encrypt=No` (Python). 3. On a non-localhost link, an ARP/DNS-spoof MITM with a self-signed cert is accepted without error.
findings.resolution: For non-dev environments set `encrypt=true;trustServerCertificate=false;hostNameInCertificate=<cn>` and provision the SQL Server CA into the JVM trust store (the prod example URL already hints at this — make it the enforced default, not a comment). For the dev scripts, gate trust-disabling behind an explicit env flag so it cannot leak into shared instances.
findings.patchAfter:
url: ${DB_URL:jdbc:sqlserver://localhost:1433;databaseName=TSS_GRC;encrypt=true;trustServerCertificate=true;sendStringParametersAsUnicode=true}
# NOTE: trustServerCertificate=true is the LOCAL-DEV default only. Non-dev DB_URL
# MUST use trustServerCertificate=false;hostNameInCertificate=<cn> with the SQL
# Server CA in the JVM trust store. application-prod.yml has no default for DB_URL,
# so prod is forced to supply a validated URL.
references: Microsoft JDBC: Connecting with SSL encryption

findings.title: Production CORS allow-list not overridden; falls back to permissive credentialed pattern matching
findings.cvss: CVSS 4.2 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — contingent on CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS being mis-set in prod; default fallback is localhost-only so direct exploitability is limited
findings.description: The base config comment states "In production, set to empty list (same-origin via Nginx reverse proxy)" and CorsConfig.java repeats that the prod profile sets `grc.cors.allowed-origins` empty. In reality `application-prod.yml` contains NO `grc.cors` block (verified — grep for cors/allowed-origins in application-prod.yml returns no matches), so prod inherits the base default `${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS:http://localhost:3000}`. Combined with `CorsConfig` using `setAllowedOriginPatterns(...)` + `setAllowCredentials(true)`, this is a documentation-vs-reality gap: the security relies entirely on the operator remembering to export `CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` correctly. Because `setAllowedOriginPatterns` treats entries as wildcard patterns (the dev profile uses `http://192.168.*:[*]`, `http://10.*:[*]`, `http://172.*:[*]` together with credentials), any over-broad value supplied via the env var in prod would allow credentialed cross-origin reads from a wide range of origins.
findings.rootCause: Prod relies on an env var the YAML never asserts, and the comment claiming an explicit empty prod list was never implemented. The pattern-matching CORS source plus allowCredentials=true makes any wildcard origin value dangerous.
findings.evidence: application-prod.yml has no `grc.cors:` key (grep returns 'No matches found'); base default at application.yml:145 — "allowed-origins: ${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS:http://localhost:3000}"; CorsConfig.java:39,43 — "config.setAllowedOriginPatterns(allowedOrigins); ... config.setAllowCredentials(true);"
findings.impact: If CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS is left unset or set to a broad pattern in production, browsers will attach the HttpOnly refresh cookie / Authorization responses for cross-origin requests from attacker-controlled origins matching the pattern, enabling session-riding data theft. With the documented intent (empty list) unimplemented, this depends on operator discipline rather than a safe default.
findings.reproduction: 1. Deploy with `--spring.profiles.active=prod` and no CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS exported. 2. Observe Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:3000 with Allow-Credentials: true on /api/** preflights. 3. Set CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS to a wildcard pattern and any matching origin can make credentialed cross-origin calls.
findings.resolution: Make prod fail-closed: add an explicit `grc.cors.allowed-origins: ${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS:}` (empty) to application-prod.yml so an unset value yields no allowed origins, and document that wildcard patterns must never be used in prod. Consider rejecting wildcard patterns when allowCredentials is true.
findings.patchBefore: # application-prod.yml — (no grc.cors block; inherits base default http://localhost:3000)
findings.patchAfter:
grc:
  cors:
    # Same-origin behind Nginx in prod -> no cross-origin allowed by default.
    # Wildcard patterns are forbidden here (allowCredentials=true is on).
    allowed-origins: ${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS:}
references: CWE-942: Permissive Cross-domain Policy with Untrusted Domains

findings.title: Dev profile ships broad LAN CORS wildcards with credentials enabled and lockout effectively disabled
findings.cvss: Risk rationale: dev-only profile, but the allowed-origin set (entire 192.168/10/172 RFC1918 space, any port) plus allowCredentials=true and 99-attempt/1-min lockout creates real exposure on shared developer LANs
findings.description: The dev profile sets `grc.cors.allowed-origins` to include `http://192.168.*:[*]`, `http://10.*:[*]`, and `http://172.*:[*]` — effectively the entire RFC1918 private address space on any port — while `CorsConfig` enables `setAllowCredentials(true)`. It also sets `max-failed-login-attempts: 99` and `lockout-duration-minutes: 1`, which disables brute-force protection. These are intentional dev conveniences (documented in CLAUDE.md and the LAN-access commits), so the rating is Low. However, when a developer runs the dev stack on a shared corporate/coffee-shop LAN with real seeded credentials (admin/Admin@12345 etc.), any other host on the subnet can host a page that makes credentialed cross-origin requests to the dev API, and the near-disabled lockout permits unlimited password guessing.
findings.rootCause: Developer-experience trade-offs (zero-config LAN access, no lockout friction) were encoded as profile defaults; they are safe only under the assumption that the dev machine is never on an untrusted network with real data.
findings.impact: On a shared LAN, a co-located attacker can (a) ride a developer's authenticated session via credentialed CORS from any RFC1918 origin, and (b) brute-force the well-known seeded passwords with no lockout. Confined to dev with throwaway data, impact is low; with production-like seed data on a laptop in public, it is meaningfully higher.
findings.reproduction: 1. Start backend with profile=dev on a machine at 192.168.1.50. 2. From 192.168.1.99, host JS that POSTs to http://192.168.1.50:8084/api/v1/... with credentials:'include' — preflight is allowed. 3. Script 200 login attempts/min against /api/v1/auth/login without triggering lockout.
findings.resolution: Keep the broad wildcards strictly behind the dev profile (already the case) and document the 'untrusted network' caveat. Prefer enumerating the developer's actual LAN IP via env var over the whole RFC1918 range, and raise the dev lockout to a non-trivial value (e.g. 20/5min) so brute-force is still slowed in dev.
findings.patchAfter:
cors:
    # Set DEV_LAN_ORIGIN to your machine's LAN URL instead of the whole RFC1918 space.
    allowed-origins: "http://localhost:3000,http://127.0.0.1:3000,${DEV_LAN_ORIGIN:}"
  security:
    max-failed-login-attempts: 20
    lockout-duration-minutes: 5
references: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts

findings.title: Well-known seeded application credentials documented and reset via committed scripts
findings.cvss: Info — intentional demo/dev credentials; dangerous only if the same accounts/passwords survive into a production deployment
findings.description: A fixed set of demo credentials following the `<Role>@12345` scheme (admin/Admin@12345, riskmanager/Risk@12345, auditor/Audit@12345, plus compliance/analyst/viewer in `.tmp/reset_pw.py`) is documented in CLAUDE.md and re-applied to `iam.users` by the committed `.tmp/reset_pw.py` script, which bcrypt-hashes each password and writes UPDATE statements. The hashing itself is sound (bcrypt, cost 10) and the script defends against quote injection in the hash (`assert "'" not in h`). This is a normal seeded-demo-account pattern and is Info-rated. The only real risk is the standard one: if these well-known accounts are not disabled/rotated before go-live, an attacker who has read the public docs can log in directly.
findings.rootCause: Predictable, publicly-documented demo passwords are convenient for development and onboarding but become a backdoor if they persist into production.
findings.impact: If demo accounts reach production unchanged, full admin takeover is trivial (admin/Admin@12345 is in the committed docs). No impact in a properly bootstrapped, separately-seeded production environment.
findings.reproduction: 1. Read CLAUDE.md credential table. 2. POST {username:'admin',password:'Admin@12345'} to /api/v1/auth/login on any environment still carrying the seed accounts -> authenticated as PLATFORM_ADMIN.
findings.resolution: Ensure the production bootstrap does NOT run the demo seed; enforce must-change-password on first login for any seeded account; add a startup guard that refuses to start in prod if a user with a known default password hash/flag exists. Keep `reset_pw.py` out of any production tooling path.
findings.patchAfter:
# Dev/demo only. In prod, seed no default users, or force must_change_password=1
# and randomise the initial password per account (do not commit it).
creds = {u: secrets.token_urlsafe(16) for u in ("auditor","rmanager",...)}
print("Generated one-time passwords:", creds)  # show once, never commit
references: OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures

findings.title: CI workflow embeds static test secrets in plaintext (env block)
findings.category: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Source Code (CWE-540)
findings.cvss: Info — values are explicitly throwaway CI-only test secrets, never used against real infrastructure
findings.description: The CI workflow defines `JWT_SECRET`, `DB_USERNAME=sa`, and `DB_PASSWORD=ci-test-Sql123!` directly in the workflow `env:` block rather than as GitHub Actions secrets. The comment correctly states these are 'Test secrets — only used inside the CI runners,' and they satisfy `JwtTokenProvider.validateSecret` (32+ chars, not a placeholder) so `mvn verify` can boot the context. Because these are deliberately disposable CI-only values with no connection to production systems, the finding is Info. The note is hygiene: putting even test secrets in workflow env (vs. repository/Org secrets) trains contributors that committing credentials is acceptable and risks a future copy-paste of a real value.
findings.rootCause: Test fixtures were inlined into the workflow for convenience; there is no policy distinguishing disposable CI values from real secrets.
findings.evidence:
.github/workflows/ci.yml:18-21 — "# Test secrets — only used inside the CI runners.
  JWT_SECRET: ci-test-secret-32-or-more-chars-not-a-placeholder-12345
  DB_USERNAME: sa
  DB_PASSWORD: ci-test-Sql123!"
findings.impact: No direct impact — the values are CI-scoped and not reused elsewhere. The residual risk is cultural/process: normalising plaintext secrets in workflow files.
findings.reproduction: 1. Open .github/workflows/ci.yml. 2. Observe JWT_SECRET/DB_PASSWORD literals in the top-level env block.
findings.resolution: Acceptable as-is given the values are throwaway. If tightening: move them to GitHub Actions repository secrets (`${{ secrets.CI_JWT_SECRET }}`) and reference there, keeping the workflow file free of literal credentials and reinforcing the no-plaintext-secrets norm.
findings.patchBefore:
env:
  JWT_SECRET: ci-test-secret-32-or-more-chars-not-a-placeholder-12345
  DB_USERNAME: sa
  DB_PASSWORD: ci-test-Sql123!
references: CWE-540: Inclusion of Sensitive Information in Source Code
GitHub Docs: Using secrets in GitHub Actions
